analysis.one_liner: Creates federal grants and background-check rules to support state red-flag gun laws.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a House vote: after its introduction it sat in the House Judiciary Committee for the rest of the two-year Congress, was sent to a subcommittee in November 2022, and died when that Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would push states and tribes to adopt 'extreme risk protection order' laws — court orders that temporarily take guns away from people judged a danger to themselves or others. It would fund training and implementation through federal grants, add people subject to such orders to the federal list of those barred from buying guns, and require courts to flag the orders in the national background-check system. It never got a floor vote in either chamber.
analysis.who_benefits: Families and communities at risk of gun suicide or violence, since the bill funds states to set up a legal process for temporarily removing firearms from people a court finds dangerous. Also tribal governments, which the bill treats as equal partners, and law enforcement agencies receiving training funds.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People at risk of gun violence

how_it_helps.text: Creates a grant program run by the Justice Department's community policing office to help states, local governments, and Indian tribes implement red-flag laws, including training for judges, court staff, health professionals, and police [S2][S3].

Requires grant recipients to fund police training on bias, domestic violence, de-escalation, and referrals to mental health and social services, and to consult domestic violence providers and suicide-prevention advocates in designing that training [S3].

Extends the existing federal prohibition on gun possession to anyone subject to a red-flag order issued with due process and a finding that the person poses a danger, so the order is enforced in the federal background-check system [S2][S3].

Requires courts to report red-flag orders to the FBI for entry into the national background-check database, and gives red-flag orders issued in one state or tribe full faith and credit in others [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Firearms dealers and manufacturers lose the sales to the narrow group of people placed under red-flag orders. Taxpayers fund the grants, whose size Congress would have had to appropriate. People subject to a court order bear the temporary loss of their firearms while the order stands.

drawbacks.text: Courts could issue an emergency 'ex parte' order without the person present; the person's hearing must come within about 30 days, and the order lasts only until then [S3].
The FBI would compile records identifying people under red-flag orders, though the bill requires destroying each record when the order expires or ends [S2][S3].
Grant eligibility depends on a state enacting a red-flag law meeting the bill's federal minimums, so states that choose not to adopt such laws receive none of this funding [S3].

A gun owner's firearms cannot be destroyed during the order without the owner's consent and must be returned once the owner regains eligibility — but the owner bears the burden of the removal and the legal process in the meantime [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The policy aims at a real, documented harm — firearm suicide and interpersonal violence by people in crisis — and the bill builds in due process protections: sworn applications, notice and a hearing, a preponderance-of-the-evidence standard, and the option of higher state standards. The cost falls on a narrow group (people individually found by a court to be dangerous) plus a small revenue loss for gun sellers, so the design is defensible on its own terms. The main weakness is that it relies on states opting in, limiting national reach.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, later sent to a subcommittee, and never received a markup or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Salud Carbajal introduced the Extreme Risk Protection Order Act of 2021 in the House on May 25, 2021 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5].
On November 1, 2022 — over a year later — it was referred to the subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, which was the last action it received [S5].
The bill drew 126 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, and no version ever passed either chamber [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who opposed new federal gun restrictions, including the gun industry and gun-rights groups, since the bill never advanced — and no state received funding, so the status quo on red-flag laws remained.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opponents of new federal gun rules

for.name: Rep. Salud Carbajal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee.

for.name: Reps. Beyer, Brownley, and Dingell
for.what_they_did: Joined Carbajal as original cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: 126 of 222 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or scheduled the bill for a floor vote in the 18 months after referral; its last action was a subcommittee referral in November 2022.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal red-flag legislation generally during this period, supporting the bill's lack of Republican cosponsors and floor action.

sides.party_line_note: All 126 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a floor vote in either chamber [S4].

industries.note: The bill bars people under red-flag orders from buying or possessing guns and requires those orders to appear in the federal background-check system, removing a small set of customers. The industry's general interest in broad access to firearms ran against the bill's goal of temporarily disarming people courts find dangerous [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Law enforcement training and consulting providers
industries.note: Grant recipients must spend 25–70 percent of funds on law-enforcement training and would procure training, protocol development, and data services, creating demand for these services. That spending serves the bill's public-safety purpose rather than profiting at the public's expense [S3].
